entries.title: How our AI Research team uses AI Runtime
entries.summary: At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to...
entries.content:
by Ethan Tang, Ivan Zhou, Irene Dea, Steven Chen, Bruce Fontaine and Ben Hansen

  • Databricks AI Research uses AI Runtime to train and fine-tune models at scale, from small experiments to workloads spanning hundreds of GPUs.
  • Built-in GPU reliability, fast job launches, and integrations with MLflow and Unity Catalog help researchers experiment faster.
  • Agent-driven research has increased training jobs 8x, with AI Runtime supporting faster, automated experimentation.

At Databricks, we continuously develop and evaluate new AI research techniques to make our products more intelligent, efficient, and useful for customers.

Our research spans products like Genie, Smart Routing, and AI Functions. Recently, we've published how we made search 3x faster, developed new techniques for offline reinforcement learning, and pushed the frontier of complex document extraction.

To build great AI models and manage hundreds of parallel research workstreams, we need infrastructure that can keep pace. That's why we use Databricks AI Runtime (AIR).

In this post, we'll share how AIR helps us experiment quickly, scale to large training workloads, and adapt to agent-led training, along with what we've learned about managing GPU resources across research projects.

Our research team develops models that power Databricks AI Functions, including 

ai_parse_document
and 
ai_extract
. For example, Databricks AI Functions deliver state-of-the-art document parsing quality, backed by models trained to understand enterprise documents. Achieving that quality requires extensive research across different architectures, datasets, training techniques, and hyperparameters, spanning tens of thousands of training and evaluation runs.

We use supervised fine-tuning (SFT), offline reinforcement learning (RL), and online RL to train models ranging from a few billion parameters to nearly a trillion. Depending on the workload, we use NVIDIA H100 or B300 GPUs, both available through AIR. Our largest training runs can require hundreds of GPUs working together over days or weeks, with high-bandwidth networking to keep training efficient.

Supporting these workloads creates three challenges:

  • Resiliency for long-running training jobs. Training can require thousands of GPU hours. A single node or RDMA network failure can leave hundreds of GPUs idle and force us to restart from an earlier checkpoint, losing hours of progress. For reinforcement learning projects like KARL, reliable infrastructure is essential.
  • Fast experimentation and prototyping. Improving AI Functions means testing thousands of approaches, from different models and training techniques to data recipes. We need to launch experiments quickly without repeatedly provisioning infrastructure or rebuilding environments.
  • GPU fleet management. We balance multiple research projects with different compute requirements, priorities, and deadlines, while remaining flexible enough to respond to new research techniques or open-source models.

Our research team has been customer zero of AI Runtime since the product's inception last year. We use AIR to develop, train, and test models that power Databricks AI products, relying on its GPU infrastructure and integration with our existing tools.

Built-in GPU resiliency

AIR performs preflight checks on assigned GPU nodes to ensure they're healthy and can communicate effectively before training starts. It also monitors node health during execution, detecting issues such as NCCL communication failures, thermal or power throttling, and GPU driver problems. If a node becomes unhealthy and causes a job to fail, AIR detects the issue and cordons off the affected node so subsequent jobs aren't scheduled on the same problematic infrastructure.

This is especially important for projects like KARL, where complex rollout generation and post-training of models with more than 100 billion parameters can require thousands of GPU hours. Rather than repeatedly troubleshooting infrastructure failures, we can focus on improving our models.

Fast iteration with the AIR CLI and custom containers

Research requires us to change model configurations, training approaches, and code frequently. With the AIR CLI, we can launch workloads programmatically, specify the GPUs we need, and let AIR handle provisioning and scheduling, including high-bandwidth networking for distributed training across clouds.

We also rely on custom Docker containers for local development. AIR lets us use those same images for training, ensuring compatibility without recreating our environments. We can upload our codebase, execute custom code in those containers, and use Databricks Artifact Registry to register and share images across experiments. AIR's investments in launch latency and container optimization help us start training jobs in seconds, shortening feedback loops as we test new ideas.

MLflow and logging for experiment tracking

We use MLflow to track our research experiments. AIR automatically creates and manages MLflow experiments for our training jobs, eliminating separate configuration.

We can monitor job status, stream and inspect training logs, and retrieve metrics to understand how experiments are progressing. This also gives our AI agents access to the information they need to evaluate results and determine what to try next.

Seamless, governed access to research data

All of our research data is stored in Unity Catalog. Through Unity Catalog FUSE mounting, AIR lets us access that data as though it were part of a local filesystem, even when working across different Databricks workspaces.

This keeps our data accessible, tracked, shareable, and governed without changing how our training code interacts with files. Combined with MLflow and our Docker-based environments, it gives us a consistent workflow from local development to distributed training.

Managing GPU capacity across research projects

Our workloads have very different resource needs. A debugging experiment may require only a few GPUs, while a large training run might need hundreds for days or weeks. Different projects also have competing timelines and priorities.

AIR's workload prioritization and preemption capabilities help us allocate resources across projects, prioritize time-sensitive experiments, and use excess capacity when it's available. For example, spare capacity can support additional exploratory experiments over a weekend without disrupting higher-priority work. Our goal is to keep GPU resources available for the experiments that matter, without requiring researchers to manually coordinate infrastructure.

Popularized by Andrej Karpathy, autoresearch is changing how we develop AI models. Instead of researchers manually launching and evaluating every experiment, we're increasingly using agents to propose changes, run experiments, evaluate results, and determine what to try next.

This shift has dramatically increased our experimentation volume. Across our AI Functions research workloads, the number of training jobs has grown by 8x.

As agents take on more of the research process, our infrastructure needs to keep up. A slow startup or confusing configuration error might be manageable when a researcher launches a handful of experiments. When agents launch hundreds, those same issues quickly become bottlenecks.

Agent-driven research requires fast job launches, programmatic interfaces, clear and actionable errors, reliable execution, and accessible training results.

Our autoresearch workflow follows a continuous cycle:

  • Propose: Agents identify potential improvements to models or training approaches.
  • Launch trials: They submit multiple experiments to AIR in parallel.
  • Learn: They evaluate training metrics to identify what improves performance.
  • Update the plan: They use the results to refine their approach and launch new experiments.

AIR is particularly well suited to this workflow because agents can interact with it programmatically and benefit from its fast job launches, built-in reliability, and ability to scale. Through the Databricks CLI and 

databricks-air-skills
, our agents can launch concurrent workloads, monitor job status, retrieve MLflow metrics, and iterate based on the results.

This lets us run more experiments while our researchers focus on developing new ideas and improving model quality. As we move further toward agent-driven research, AIR gives us the infrastructure to support both larger models and a faster pace of experimentation.

Our experience using AI Runtime has shown us how much reliable, flexible GPU infrastructure matters for research. From large-scale training and governed data access to agent-driven experimentation, AIR lets us spend less time managing infrastructure and more time developing better models.

If you're training or fine-tuning your own models, check out the AI Runtime documentation to get started.

AI Runtime has also powered our research across areas like faster search, reinforcement learning, and document understanding. Explore more of our work at Databricks AI Research,

entries.title: Reducing the noise: How Atlassian built an OCSF security lakehouse on Databricks
entries.summary: The challenge: Two decades of logging noise at global scaleAtlassian is a global...
entries.content:
Facing 44 billion events a day, Atlassian standardized security logs on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and built a self-service security lakehouse on Databricks — cutting ingestion costs and powering 500+ threat-detection signals.

by Taylor Kain, Zachary Schmerber (Atlassian) and Niels Heijmans (Atlassian)

  • 80% reduction in ingestion cost after standardizing security telemetry on OCSF
  • 500+ production threat-detection signals running on a single, unified schema
  • 60% increase in analyst productivity — one repeatable process across every tool
  • Up to 95% faster queries (from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds) using OCSF structure
  • 44 billion events per day normalized into a common schema
  • Winner of the Databricks 2026 Transformation Award

Atlassian is a global SaaS provider serving 350,000 customers — the product of 20 years of growth and a long list of acquisitions, each of which arrived with its own logging formats. The result was a security data pipeline absorbing 44 billion events per day with no common language across various log sources.

"You've got varied timestamps, you've got proprietary schemas, you've got operational drain for anyone trying to organize and structure this information," explained Zachary Schmerber, Senior Security Logging Engineer at Atlassian and a maintainer of the OCSF schema. Analysts were burning time normalizing data after it landed, cross-platform correlation was limited because data lived in different places and shapes, and SIEM pipelines were not keeping pace.

The team needed a way to coalesce fragmented telemetry into one place and make sense of it, while maintaining flexibility and avoiding vendor lock-in.

Atlassian's answer was to standardize everything on the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) and build the lakehouse on Databricks.

OCSF won because it was the only option the team considered wholly open. Compared to alternatives like ECS or UDM, it offered a strongly typed schema with robust validation that minimized ambiguity after transformation, good compression efficiency, extensibility, and an open-source community (with Linux Foundation backing and a path toward international standardization). Its roughly 40,000 fields looked daunting at first — but that verbosity turned out to be the platform's greatest asset, because the semantic context stays with the data.

"Investigations where a single query could hit many different data sources — because the data is structured," said Schmerber. "Maybe you've got five vulnerability scanners in your system. Now you have one data set instead of five."

Databricks was the natural platform. Native ACID transactions made it far easier to migrate across schema versions without breaking downstream consumers; auto-scaling Spark clusters handled shared, high-volume workloads; and the platform was built to manage the infrastructure overhead of a large, multi-team organization. Atlassian deliberately chose ETL over ELT — transforming data in flight — to enable real-time detection, preserve vendor independence, and compress data as it moved through the pipeline.

Table optimization delivered dramatic performance gains. With structured OCSF data, partitioning and Z-ORDER took a representative query from ~45 seconds to 2–3 seconds — a 95% improvement, with similar gains on larger queries. Enabling Graviton clusters with Photon cut query cost and runtime by roughly two-thirds.

A defining engineering decision was embedding the entire OCSF schema into Go structs — what the team calls "TypeGo." Because the schema lives in the type system, correctness is guaranteed at compile time.

"Every time you produce a new OCSF log, it's pre-validated — because it can't be anything but OCSF," said Schmerber. Nested objects are native, deployments can run anywhere, and everything is unit tested. Crucially, this type safety also tamed AI: when the team automated transformation with an agentic workflow, the rigid schema sharply reduced hallucinations and cut token usage, because the agent couldn't produce invalid mappings and cycle through bad iterations.

The biggest transformation was operational. Atlassian's security data-engineering team started with a six-phase manual procedure to collect logs, transform them into TypeGo, route, test, configure, and ship them via PR. Over time they automated nearly all of it — and eventually handed it back to the customer as a self-service platform.

Now an analyst identifies the logs they want and provides a canonical dataset. After a gated confirmation, the workflow scans the framework inside the Go structs, generates the mappings and the DAG, tests them locally, deploys a canary configuration via PR, validates at scale in a canary environment, and — after a soak — gets promoted to production and notifies the user of any errors. Regression testing gates everything before production.

The tool chain includes a schema-mapping IDE and an open-source Go OCSF library with validation performance enhancements, automatic handling of unmapped fields, schema helpers (IP path, normalization), and intelligent routing. The payoff is low onboarding overhead: "I can now have a SOC analyst do principal data engineer work in a production environment," said Schmerber — with every change still reviewed.

The acceleration is stark: "It took me a year to map about one-third of the data we have mapped today," Schmerber noted, "and two months to map the other two-thirds."

For the detection and response team, standardization changed how alerts get written. "Adopting the OCSF schema has enabled us to transform our threat detection pipeline by moving from one-to-one alerts to a signal- and risk-based detection methodology, where multiple signal findings are clustered together in a single alert," said Jordan of Atlassian's Detection and Response team.

Using a custom tool called Alert Explorer, findings cluster around standardized OCSF values — for example, a single 

actor.user
value that is identical whether it appears in an authentication event or a network event. That consistency lets the team standardize clustering, enrichment, and triage plays: instead of per-detection enrichment, they call an enrichment API on a standardized username value every time.

"OCSF has made it much easier to write detections and provide more meaningful, actionable alerts," said Jordan, "which analysts can dive deep into regardless of where the data came from."

Beyond the headline cost and performance numbers, standardization unlocked capabilities that were previously impractical: multi-domain correlation with strong entity resolution, efficient user-behavior analytics, and cross-application pattern analysis. With everything speaking one language, the team could write simple queries to spot anomalous behavior across five different routers — or five vulnerability scanners — at once. Dashboards were simplified dramatically because OCSF classes share objects, and storage was optimized because the team knew what data to keep and what to drop.

Schmerber is most excited about what the semantically rich schema unlocks for AI. "How do you talk to your data unless your agent has context? It'll hallucinate and give you the wrong answer," he said. Because OCSF carries its definitions inside the schema, agentic assistance becomes far more accurate.

The roadmap includes skills training that feeds an analyst's real field usage into reusable agent skills, an orchestration of agents that can run threat hunts with the right context, contextual SQL that can answer questions like "where's my DNS C2 traffic in this schema?", and context graphs built on OCSF. The longer-term ambition is semantic: making OCSF the canonical starting point that everything emits — rather than a model coalesced from data after the fact. The team will also continue with improving query performance by looking at a move to Liquid Clustering for data partitioning across environments like corporate devices and cloud.

entries.summary: Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on Lakehouse//RT and they're up to 38X faster...
entries.content:
Lakehouse//RT delivers ultra low latency spatial queries at scale

by Kent Marten, Matt Slack and Kaitlin Baumgardner

  • Spatial SQL and spatial joins are now supported on Lakehouse//RT, delivering ultra low latency and high concurrency directly on your governed lakehouse data.
  • Benchmarks show Lakehouse//RT delivers 38X faster spatial query performance than a traditional data warehouse with 50 concurrent users.
  • No separate geospatial serving layer required. Spatial SQL on Lakehouse//RT combines real-time performance with open formats, Unity Catalog governance, and the full 100+ spatial function library.

Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on Lakehouse//RT and they're up to 38X faster than traditional cloud data warehouses.

Earlier this year, we brought Spatial SQL to General Availability on Databricks: this included support for the GEOMETRY data type, 100+ spatial functions, high-performance spatial joins, AI/BI maps, Delta Sharing. The GEOMETRY and GEOGRAPHY data types are part of the open lakehouse, available in Apache Spark, and supported in the same underlying parquet files used by Delta and Iceberg v3. Customers across insurance, agriculture, energy, telecom, retail, logistics and more have adopted it to consolidate geospatial workloads onto a single governed platform.

Organizations with both spatial OLAP workloads and real-time location-based applications want great performance and high concurrency. Many of these organizations still rely on traditional data warehouses and build out specialized architectures for spatial applications, sometimes managing a separate stack centered on PostGIS for every use case just to meet latency requirements. Separate stacks lead to more copies of data, more synchronization pipelines, and more governance overhead.

Databricks now supports 4-pillars for geospatial workloads: Lakehouse for long-running spatial OLAP workloads, Lakebase for spatial OLTP, apps, and agents, Databricks Apps for purpose-built experiences, and now the Lakehouse//RT warehouse for real-time analytics. 

This blog covers what Lakehouse//RT delivers for spatial workloads, driving up to 38X performance improvement under high concurrency.

We benchmarked Lakehouse//RT against a traditional cloud data warehouse across a suite of spatial queries using SpatialBench. By comparison, Lakehouse//RT delivers 3X faster on average, and up to 20X faster across the tested queries.

Under heavy load, the performance differences are even more significant. At 50 concurrent users, Lakehouse//RT delivers up to 38X on the queries where the traditional warehouse could keep up.

Try it for yourself: Follow the SpatialBench documentation to generate the synthetic data used in the benchmark queries from this page.

Take a look at query #8. To follow best practices, it is recommended to remove the ST_GeomFromWKB call that converts data stored as well-known binary and instead use the native GEOMETRY data types. Using the native data types allows query optimizations and file-skipping to provide the best performance.

Three takeaways:

  • Lakehouse//RT is up to 38X faster, maintaining performance with high-concurrency. Even removing the most significant query improvement; the average speed-up is over 3.5X.
  • Lakehouse//RT is up to 20X faster with single-query concurrency. Every spatial benchmark query is faster on Lakehouse//RT.
  • No query changes or new licenses required. Spatial workloads are portable on Databricks; the same spatial queries you run on SQL Serverless today can run on Lakehouse//RT with no code changes.

Spatial SQL on Databricks already serves a wide range of industries. With Lakehouse//RT, workloads can run with the real-time speed applications demand. Here are a few examples:

  • Telecom and retail: Evaluate subscriber signal health in coverage areas and assess trade-area overlap for new store sites.
  • Energy and natural resources: Intersect well locations against land leases, pipeline routes against suitability corridors, and renewable sites against terrain and infrastructure.
  • Insurance and risk: Match policies to projected storm paths and calculate insured value at risk, provide real-time forecast updates to reinsurance partners.
  • Logistics and delivery: Assign orders to the nearest service area instantly.
  • Security and observability: Correlate threat signals with geographic boundaries and serve point-in-polygon lookups to dashboards and agents at high concurrency.

Spatial SQL on Lakehouse//RT is available now in Beta. To get started:

  • Create a Lakehouse//RT real-time warehouse from the SQL Warehouses page
  • Run your existing spatial queries; no code changes needed
  • Explore the Spatial SQL documentation for the full function reference

At Data + AI Summit 2026, we introduced Lakehouse//RT, Databricks' new real-time data warehouse built to deliver millisecond query performance at massive concurrency directly on your lakehouse data. Lakehouse//RT was designed to solve a specific problem: as organizations expand data access across users, applications, dashboards, and AI agents, they need real-time responsiveness without copying data into a separate serving layer. Preview customers have seen significantly better performance overall with Lakehouse//RT vs. real-time serving layers, with latency as low as 10ms and concurrency as high as 12,000 queries per second.

Yes. Spatial SQL and spatial joins now run on the Lakehouse//RT, so you can serve geospatial queries with low latency and high concurrency directly on your governed Delta and Iceberg tables. There is no need to copy data into a separate geospatial system or real-time analytics serving layer.

No. The same spatial functions and spatial joins you run on Databricks SQL Serverless today run on Lakehouse//RT with no code changes. You get the speedup by creating a Lakehouse//RT warehouse and pointing your existing queries at it.

In head-to-head benchmarks against a traditional data warehouse, Lakehouse//RT runs spatial queries up to 38X faster under heavy load. On average, benchmark queries are 3.5X faster even when you exclude the largest increase.

Spatial SQL and spatial joins are available on Lakehouse//RT in Beta. To get started, create a Lakehouse//RT warehouse from the SQL Warehouses page and run your existing spatial queries with no code changes.

Yes. All H3 expressions supported by Databricks Lakehouse are supported today with Lakehouse//RT. Read more about H3 here.

Yes. You can create maps that use native geometry and geography data types in AI/BI dashboards. Read more here.

entries.title: Sizing Lakebase Search: lessons from a real app and 4 million passages
entries.summary: Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse...
entries.content:
• Lakebase Search runs vector and BM25 keyword search as Postgres extensions inside the application database, so developers get hybrid search without maintaining a separate search system or a second transaction path.
  • Benchmarks show that sizing the Local File Cache to roughly match the vector index keeps 95~98% of pages in memory, dropping warm vector latency to single-digit milliseconds, while reducing the candidate pool from 1,000 to 200 preserves 90.5% of top-10 results at one-third the page reads.
  • Lakebase Postgres bills compute only while it runs, and a 14-minute load test serving 109k requests used just $0.02 of Lakebase Postgres compute, making a $31~40/month always-on 0.5 CU floor the recommended production baseline to avoid cold starts.

Slide Hub is an internal Databricks app. Field engineers use it to find and reuse slides from about 700 internal presentations: event talks, product decks, and architecture decks. A search bar finds single slides by meaning and by keyword, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives AI agents the same search. The app stores its slides, votes, search telemetry, and change history in Lakebase Postgres. We use Slide Hub as the baseline to benchmark Lakebase Postgres. It is a real app with a real use case and real users, so its numbers show how the database behaves under an actual workload.

This post is for developers and architects who build apps on Databricks and want search inside the app's own Lakebase Postgres database. It assumes that you know SQL and the basics of PostgreSQL. If you plan a search bar or an agent tool on Lakebase Postgres, the numbers below help you choose the compute size before you go to production.

This post shows how Slide Hub runs search inside Lakebase Postgres, what limits it under load, what it costs, and how Lakebase Search behaves from 1M to 4M rows of a public corpus.

Lakebase Search became generally available in September. It is a set of Postgres extensions, so it runs next to the application tables. The app does not copy data to a separate search system. The developer does not maintain a second transaction path.

Two 

CREATE EXTENSION
statements enable the components. 
lakebase_vector
stores embeddings, vectors of numbers that represent the meaning of a text, and supports the 
lakebase_ann
index for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search. 
lakebase_text
supports the 
lakebase_bm25
index for BM25, a standard method that ranks text by the query words it contains. 
lakebase_tokenizer
is optional. The ANN index uses IVF partitioning, which groups similar vectors so a query reads only a few groups, and RaBitQ quantization, which compresses each vector to about 1 bit per dimension. BM25 scores text with the <@> operator.

Slide Hub’s 23k slide rows sit in the same serverless Lakebase Postgres instance as the votes, telemetry, change history, previews, and both indexes. The app reads the data and the indexes inside one connection and one permission model.

Slide Hub runs hybrid search. It combines vector search, which finds slides with a similar meaning to the query, and BM25 keyword search, which finds slides that contain the query words. Each method returns a short list of its best matches, the candidates. One SQL statement carries the whole ranking policy. It ranks each candidate list, fuses the two rankings, applies the app filters, and joins the votes. Search and app logic share one connection, one set of grants, and one commit.

Slide Hub takes 200 candidates from each method. It fuses the two lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) at k=60: a slide scores 1/(60 + its rank) in each list, and the two scores add. A similarity gate of 0.70 rejects vector matches that are too far from the query to be useful for this embedding model. Title tiers add weight when the query matches a slide title. Notes receive weight 0.5. Scope filters restrict the result to assets the user has permission to see.

A search request uses two separate computes, and either one can set the limit.

Lakebase Postgres compute runs the database. Lakebase Postgres sizes it in Compute Units (CU). One CU allocates about 2 GB of RAM to the database, with its share of CPU and local SSD. A compute autoscales between a minimum and a maximum size from 0.5 CU to 64 CU, and the maximum can be at most 16 CU above the minimum. Fixed-size computes go up to 112 CU, and computes up to 32 CU can scale to zero.Postgres stores tables and indexes in 8 KB pages. Lakebase Postgres keeps recently read pages in a Local File Cache (LFC) on the compute. The cache grows with the CU size and can use up to 75% of the compute's memory. A page that is not in the cache comes from storage, which takes longer.

Databricks Apps compute runs the Slide Hub web server. Its size is fixed per app. A MEDIUM app has up to 2 vCPU and 6 GB of memory, and a LARGE app has up to 4 vCPU and 12 GB. Slide Hub runs one app instance. Each Python worker process in it holds a pool of 8 database connections, so 2 workers open at most 16 connections and 4 workers open at most 32.

For each request, the app embeds the query text, sends one SQL statement to Lakebase Postgrse, and returns the result. To find the limit, the test changes one side at a time. It pins Lakebase Postgres at one CU size and changes the app, or it keeps the app and changes the CU size. A load generator simulates users that send search requests, and it raises the number of users in steps. The list shows requests per second and the median latency (p50) at 500 users for each Lakebase Postgres size and app size.

  • 1 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 196 req/s, p50 1.8 s
  • 0.5 to 1 CU, LARGE app with 4 workers: 193 req/s, p50 1.6 s
  • 2 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 201 req/s, p50 1.8 s
  • 4 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 219 req/s, p50 1.6 s
  • 8 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 336 req/s, p50 1.0 s
  • 16 CU, MEDIUM app with 2 workers: 349 req/s, p50 1.0 s
  • 16 CU, LARGE app with 4 workers: at least 662 req/s, p50 343 ms

Up to 4 CU, Lakebase is the limit. A LARGE app with twice the workers and connections adds nothing at 1 CU. At 1 CU the search statement averaged 146 ms and read 14.9M pages from storage, with a file cache of 1.5 GB. At 8 CU it averaged 34 ms, with a cache of 12 GB, and throughput rose about 50%.

From 8 CU, the app is the limit. 16 CU with the same MEDIUM app adds only 4%, and its database connections sit mostly idle. A LARGE app with 4 workers at 16 CU reaches at least 662 req/s, and there the load generator was the limit. Size the query first. Then scale Lakebase Postgres until the app workers are the limit, and then scale the app.

Takeaway: Find the limit before you scale. Below 8 CU, add Lakebase Postgres CU. From 8 CU, give the app more workers.

The connection pool is still necessary. At 50 users the app reached 45 req/s and 2.4 s p95 without the pool, and 85 req/s and 0.7 s p95 with it. The embedding cache made no measurable difference under load.

The candidate limit sets the number of pages a query touches. On a cold cache, that number sets the latency. Slide Hub shipped with 1,000 candidates per method. The docs pattern uses 40. The candidate-limit experiment changed only candidate_limit and measured 20 public queries in three states. Cold is the first query after the compute scaled to zero, with an empty cache. First-touch is the first run of a query on an awake compute. Repeat is the same query run again, with its pages in the cache. Pages touched counts the pages a query reads from any source. Top-10 overlap is the share of the top 10 results that match the result at 1,000 candidates.

  • 40 candidates: cold 127 ms, first-touch 13 ms, repeat 5.0 ms. Touches 5,655 pages. Top-10 overlap 74.5%.
  • 100 candidates: cold 240 ms, first-touch 16 ms, repeat 7.9 ms. Touches 7,355 pages. Top-10 overlap 89%.
  • 200 candidates: cold 387 ms, first-touch 24 ms, repeat 11.7 ms. Touches 10,401 pages. Top-10 overlap 90.5%.
  • 1,000 candidates: cold 740 ms, first-touch 109 ms, repeat 35.3 ms. Touches 28,972 pages. Top-10 overlap 100% (the reference).

At 200 candidates, 90.5% of the top 10 stays the same, and the reported number of matches is 81% of the number at 1,000 candidates. Users rarely page past 200 results, so Slide Hub now ships 200. Measured end to end from a job in the same cloud region as the app, a cold search at 200 candidates took 2.9 s, and a repeat search took 40 ms. The cold time has two parts. The connection waits about 1 s while the endpoint wakes up. Then each query reads its pages from storage until the cache warms. The first query on a new connection also pays about 75 ms of planning.

Takeaway: Keep the candidate pool small. 200 candidates keep 90.5% of the top 10 results, read about a third of the pages of 1,000 candidates, and halve the cold latency.

The scale tests use MIRACL English, a passage corpus built from Wikipedia. The full corpus has 32,893,221 passages. We embedded it with gte-large-en-v1.5, a 1024-dimension open model, the same size as the Slide Hub embeddings. We self-hosted the model on one A10G GPU at 379 passages per second. The whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the same work on a model-serving endpoint. The GPU vectors matched the endpoint vectors (mean cosine 1.0000, minimum 0.9978).

We built three subsets: 1M, 2M, and 4M passages. The lakebase_ann index grew with the corpus: 5.8 GB at 1M, 11.5 GB at 2M, 23.0 GB at 4M. A binary COPY loaded all 4M rows in 19 minutes at 8 CU.

Lakebase Postgres holds about 1.6 GB of file cache per CU. Scale raises one question: what happens when the index is larger than the cache? Each test cell is one corpus size at one CU size, so the cache is a known fraction of the index. We call that fraction the cache ratio: cache size divided by vector index size. A ratio of 1.0 means the index just fits. The hit rate is the share of the pages a query reads that do not come from storage.

We ran three query mixes against each cell. The uniform mix sends a new title every time and never repeats, the worst case for a cache. The skewed mix draws from a pool of 20,000 titles with a Zipf distribution, a common model for search traffic. The cold mix runs the first queries right after a wake-up, when the cache is empty. Before the uniform and skewed measurements, a warm-up runs the same mix until the hit rate stops changing. We call the results after the warm-up warm.

The hit rate depends on the cache ratio. The corpus size does not change it: the 2M and 4M points fall on one curve. At a ratio of 0.07 the skewed mix hit 45% of its pages in cache. At 0.57 it hit 86%. At 1.14, where the index just fits, it hit 97%. The uniform mix sits a few points lower, because it reuses nothing.

That gives a sizing rule. Measure your index size, pick a CU size for the cache ratio you want, and read the hit rate off the curve. The ratio works across corpus sizes, so a test at 2M predicts the behavior at 4M.

Takeaway: Size the cache from the vector index, not from the row count. A cache about as large as the index serves 95% to 98% of the pages without storage.

Warm vector p50 fell from 187 ms at a ratio of 0.07 to 4 ms at a ratio of 2.3. Hybrid search stayed near 800 ms until the ratio approached 1, then dropped to 33 ms. The keyword half of the hybrid query reads the most pages, so it gains the most from a full cache.

Takeaway: Vector search takes 160 to 230 ms while the cache holds less than a third of the index, and 11 to 23 ms once the whole index fits.

A miss is one 8 KB Postgres page that is not in the Local File Cache. In the vector index, one page holds one or two embeddings. One page read from storage costs a fixed amount of time. Across every measured query, execution time grows by about 252 microseconds per missed page for vector search and 316 for hybrid. A query that misses 2,000 pages pays about half a second. A full cache removes almost all the misses. This is why the cache ratio sets the latency: it sets how many pages each query reads from storage.

Takeaway: Each page from storage adds about 0.3 ms. Multiply the storage misses per query by 0.3 ms to estimate what the cache saves you.

Hold the cache ratio near 1.0 and change the corpus size. Warm vector latency stayed between 11 and 23 ms from 1M to 4M. Warm hybrid latency stayed near 276 ms. The cold queries, which read from storage, grew with the corpus: a cold vector query went from 44 ms at 1M to 133 ms at 4M, and a cold hybrid query reached 911 ms at 4M.

This is the honest form of “you do not need the whole index in memory”: you do not, because the architecture keeps compute memory flat. RaBitQ stores about 1 bit per dimension, 32 times smaller than float32, and IVF reads only a few partitions per query. The index is storage-backed, so compute can be small or scale to zero. The queries that miss the cache pay for the miss, and the cache ratio controls how often that happens.

Takeaway: Grow the compute with the corpus, and warm latency stays flat. Only the queries that miss the cache get slower as the corpus grows.

The throughput test sent hybrid queries straight to Lakebase Postgres, without the app, so it measures the database alone. It opened 1, 4, 16, or 64 connections to Lakebase Postgres at the same time. Each connection sent a query, waited for the answer, and then sent the next one. The chart shows the total number of queries per second across all connections. When a line goes flat, more connections do not finish more queries. Lakebase Postgres is then at its limit, and each query waits longer instead. The load generator's own CPU stayed near zero, so Lakebase Postgres set every number.

On the 4M corpus the skewed mix reached about 4 queries per second at 2 CU, 15 at 8 CU, and 65 at 16 CU. At 64 connections, the median wait for one query was 14.5 s at 2 CU, 5.2 s at 8 CU, and 343 ms at 16 CU. The uniform mix at 16 CU peaked at 30 queries per second, because it never reuses a page. Throughput scales with the compute size and the cache ratio together.

Read these as the cost of cache misses under load. Most queries in a real app repeat or cluster, so the warm hit rate, not the uniform mix, sets steady-state capacity.

Takeaway: More CU buys throughput twice, with more CPU and a larger cache. Going from 8 CU to 16 CU raised the skewed throughput from 15 to 65 queries per second.

The lakebase_ann index is approximate. Recall@10 is the share of the true 10 nearest passages, from an exact search over all vectors, that the index also returns. The index splits the vectors into partitions (IVF), and lakebase_ann.probes sets how many partitions a query reads. Recall@10 barely moved with the corpus size at the default probe count: 0.74 at 1M, 0.75 at 2M, and 0.75 at 4M. More probes trade latency for recall.

With the default index at 4M, the default 109 probes gave a recall@10 of 0.74 in 3 ms, and 2,000 probes gave 0.95 in 49 ms. An index built with build_mode = 'quality' raised recall at every probe count: 0.80 at the default probes in 3 ms, and 0.97 at 2,000 probes in about the same time as the default build. Its build took 52 minutes at 16 CU. Raising lakebase_ann.epsilon to 4, the highest value it accepted in our tests, added less than 0.3 points.[9] Recall depends on the data and the embedding model, so measure it on your own data and pick the probe count your app needs. Lakebase Search supports a single index of over 1 billion vectors.[1]

Takeaway: Build the vector index with build_mode = 'quality'. At the default probes it raised recall@10 from 0.74 to 0.80 in about 3 ms, and at 500 probes it reached 0.91 in 13 ms, which takes 1,000 probes and 20 ms on the default build. The cost is the build time: 52 minutes for 4M passages at 16 CU. Raise the probes only if your app needs more recall.

Lakebase cost follows use. A suspended compute incurs no compute cost, and storage is billed separately. Lakebase was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. Slide Hub is an internal app, and a slower first search after 5 idle minutes is acceptable for its users, so its production database scales to zero when nobody searches.

The scale evaluation was cheap. The self-hosted embedding of the whole corpus took 2.95 GPU-hours, against $48.87 for the model-serving endpoint. One in-region load ramp ran for 14 minutes and cost $0.13 at list price: $0.11 for the app and $0.02 for Lakebase Postgres, which autoscaled between 0.5 and 1 CU and used 0.21 CU-hours. Up to 1,000 users the ramp served 109,602 requests without errors. The cells ran at 0.5 to 16 CU and suspended between runs. In our workspace's billing tables, one CU-hour is 0.213 DBU: about $0.085 at the Premium list price and $0.11 at the Enterprise list price in AWS US East.

Takeaway: Lakebase Postgres bills compute only while it runs. The 14-minute load test used $0.02 of Lakebase Postgres compute, and that compute cost was about 1% of the Slide Hub 30-day bill. For production, set the minimum to 0.5 CU instead of scaling to zero. At list price that costs about $31 to $40 a month, and searches no longer wait about 1 s for the compute to wake or start with an empty cache.[11] Let dev and test branches scale to zero.

MIRACL English is open. The corpus is Apache-2.0, and its passages come from Wikipedia under CC BY-SA. The embedding model gte-large-en-v1.5 is Apache-2.0.This post reports aggregate metrics only. The same test runs with any 1024-dimension model: swap the embedding step, keep the table, the indexes, and the search.

Think of Lakebase Postgres as a reader at a desk in front of a large bookshelf.

  • The bookshelf is storage, and the desk is the cache. Pages on the desk are fast to read. Pages on the shelf take a walk, about 0.3 ms each.
  • Make the desk as large as the books you use. When the cache is about as large as the vector index, almost every page is on the desk, and a vector search takes milliseconds.
  • More CU gives a larger desk and more hands. That makes each search faster and lets Lakebase Postgres answer more searches at the same time.
  • Ask for fewer books. A search that takes 200 candidates instead of 1,000 carries about a third of the pages and keeps 9 of the top 10 results.
  • Sort the shelves well, then choose how many to search. An index built in quality mode returns 8 of the true 10 nearest passages at the default probes in 3 ms, and 97 of 100 with 2,000 probes in about 50 ms.
  • The app has its own desk. Once Lakebase Postgres is fast, the app’s workers become the limit. Then give the app more workers. More Lakebase Postgres CU does not help at that point.
  • You do not need the whole library on the desk. Lakebase Postgres reads the rest from storage. It is slower, but it works, and the cache ratio tells you how often it happens.
  • You pay for the desk only while someone reads. When nobody searches, Lakebase Postgres can suspend and bill only storage; in Slide Hub it was about 1% of the 30-day bill. In production, keep a small desk open: 0.5 CU costs about $31 to $40 a month and avoids the cold start.

Databricks has three searches, and each one fits a different job. Pick the one that sits next to your data.

  • Lakebase Search runs inside the app's Postgres database. Use it when the search must live next to the app's own tables and see each write at once.
  • AI Search, formerly Vector Search, is a managed search service over Lakehouse tables in Unity Catalog. It keeps its index in sync with a Delta or Iceberg table and can create the embeddings for you. Use it for RAG, agents, and recommendations over Lakehouse data.
  • Full-text search indexes (Beta) speed up SQL queries on managed Delta and Iceberg tables. The search and isearch functions use the index to skip files that cannot contain a match, so log and keyword lookups read less data. They filter rows and do not rank results for a search bar.

Slide Hub runs all of this in one Lakebase Postgres database: the app data, the vector index, and the keyword index. Start with the Lakebase Search docs, then run the same test against your own data.

entries.content:
Predictive AI Functions give business users and SQL analysts high-quality forecasting, anomaly detection, driver analysis, and prediction — without advanced ML expertise.

by Jonathan Brito and Gary Shambat

  • Predictive AI Functions let business users and SQL analysts create forecasts, detect anomalies, analyze what's driving a metric, and make predictions — all without advanced ML expertise.
  • AI Functions are easy to use in Genie and embed in existing workflows without requiring users to build and maintain models
  • The launch includes five functions: an upgraded ai_forecast, plus the new ai_top_drivers, ai_detect_anomalies, ai_predict_value, and ai_predict_class.

Data teams all get asked the same questions: "what will sales be next quarter?," "why did this metric move?," and "is this recent data outside the norm of what we typically see?" Answering these advanced analytics questions usually means handing the work to a data science team to build models and manage infrastructure. This creates a bottleneck where business users wait in line and many questions never even get asked.

Predictive AI Functions, now in Beta, remove that bottleneck by letting analysts and business users run advanced analytics like forecasting, driver analysis, and anomaly detection, all through built-in functions backed by state-of-the-art ML models. These SQL-native functions can be called directly in SQL, invoked in Genie with plain-language questions, or embedded in dashboards. Because Databricks maintains the models centrally, teams get high-quality, consistent answers without building or managing infrastructure.

This launch adds four new SQL native functions and improved accuracy to 

ai_forecast
: 
  • ai_forecast
    : project a time series into the future
  • ai_top_drivers
    : find which segments most drove a change in a metric
  • ai_detect_anomalies
    : flag outlier rows in temporal data
  • ai_predict_value
    : predict continuous values (regression)
  • ai_predict_class
    : predict categorical values (classification)

To showcase how these functions can be used across Databricks, we'll walk through examples in dashboards, SQL, and Genie using the NYC taxi trips dataset.

Dashboards are where teams watch the metrics that run their business, and often where they turn to see where those metrics are headed next. With 

ai_forecast
, teams can project metrics and surface those forecasts alongside the rest of their reporting.

The new 

ai_forecast
makes it easy to get high-quality forecasts without any tuning. It's powered by a transformer-based time series foundation model, pretrained on a huge, diverse collection of time series the way a large language model is trained on text. Because it already recognizes common patterns like seasonality and trends, it produces accurate forecasts on your data with no tuning required.

The visualization below uses 

ai_forecast
to project the monthly ride volumes in the NYC taxi trips dataset through the end of 2027. The forecast reveals expected seasonal patterns in taxi demand, providing a data-driven view of where ridership is headed.

The new 

ai_forecast
not only handles general patterns automatically, it also introduces features to let teams add factors specific to their business. With built-in holiday support, teams can automatically account for local events like Christmas dips and school-holiday spikes. Teams can also specify external covariates, feeding in the factors that drive a metric, such as pricing changes or marketing spend, so forecasts better reflect their business.

This launch also introduces four new functions for the ad-hoc advanced analytics questions commonly asked by data teams.

  • ai_top_drivers
    explains why a metric moved
  • ai_detect_anomalies
    flags values that look off
  • ai_predict_value
    and 
    ai_predict_class
    fill in missing values by estimating a number or assigning a category.

Each one, like 

ai_forecast
, is a native SQL function. Analysts can call them directly in the SQL editor or a notebook, run them across hundreds of millions of rows, and feed the results into their queries and pipelines alongside the rest of their work. Compared to developing custom models for similar functionality, this compresses development time and increases accessibility to more users.

For example, the query below aggregates NYC taxi trips into a daily revenue time series and passes it to 

ai_detect_anomalies
, which automatically fits a model to the data and flags unusual days.

These same functions will be available to business users through Genie (

ai_top_drivers
is available today, with
 ai_forecast
,
 ai_detect_anomalies
, 
ai_predict_value
, and
 ai_predict_class
coming soon). Anyone can ask a question in plain language, like why revenue dropped last quarter or which customers are likely to churn, and Genie calls the right function to return a grounded, model-backed answer, with no SQL or ML expertise required.

The query below uses 

ai_top_drivers
to automatically identify which time-of-day and weekday/weekend segments contributed the most to the change in NYC taxi fare revenue between January and February 2016. It ranks each segment by its absolute and relative revenue impact, revealing that weekday midday hours drove the largest gain while the weekday evening rush was the biggest drag.

Because these functions use tailored machine learning methods, they enable Genie to answer questions a general-purpose LLM cannot reliably handle on its own.

These functions all deliver high-quality predictions backed by production-grade ML models. Because Databricks maintains those models centrally, that quality stays consistent across every surface, so teams get the same trustworthy result whether a prediction runs in a dashboard, in SQL, or through Genie.

Forecasting shows this most concretely. We used fev-bench to benchmark the new ai_forecast against functions from a leading cloud data warehouse. Task win rate is defined as the percentage of tasks (measured by scaled quantile loss) where one system achieves a lower probabilistic error than the other. Here's how the options compare:

ai_forecast
outperforms other cloud data warehouse providers as well as the previous version of 
ai_forecast
. With Predictive AI Functions, teams get industry-leading accuracy out of the box, on every surface, with no tuning required.

Predictive AI Functions turn questions that once required a data science team, like what's next, why did it change, what's wrong, and what's the value, into answers business teams can get themselves, right where they already work: in dashboards, in Genie, and in SQL. The result is advanced analytics for everyone: high-quality predictions that are easy to use, with no models to build or infrastructure to manage.

Ready to try it? Get started with Predictive AI Functions here.

entries.title: How FactSet cut model training and deployment from days to hours with Databricks AI Runtime
entries.summary: FactSet’s Text-to-Formula (TTF) system has a deceptively difficult job: take a natural-language...
entries.content:
FactSet uses fine-tuned open models to power “Text To Formula (TTF)”, turning natural-language requests into FactSet Query Language while retraining every few weeks as new data becomes available.

by Nikhil Hiriyur Sunderraj, Dakshina Murthy Malladi, Nikitha Goram, Ryan Roser, Kate Stepp, Julia Powell, Tejas Sundaresan and Lucas de Paula

  • FactSet’s Text-to-Formula (TTF) system converts natural-language requests from investment professionals into FactSet Query Language (FQL) formulas. After an initial RAG approach hit a quality ceiling on complex formulas, FactSet made fine-tuned open models a core part of the architecture.
  • The team retrains models every two to three weeks as new data becomes available, making infrastructure setup and deployment speed important parts of the development cycle.
  • With Databricks AI Runtime, FactSet can select serverless GPU compute for each workload and train alongside its existing Lakehouse workflows, reducing the time to set up, train, and deploy a model from days to hours.

FactSet’s Text-to-Formula (TTF) system has a deceptively difficult job: take a natural-language request from an investment professional and turn it into the correct FactSet Query Language (FQL) formula.

FactSet initially built TTF around retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), using retrieval to find relevant examples and information for a given request. But as consumption grew, queries became more specialized and formulas more complex; the approach hit a quality ceiling. FactSet began incorporating fine-tuned open models into its Compound AI architecture, allowing the team to train models on the structure and patterns of FQL rather than relying primarily on retrieval at inference time. In its earlier work on TTF, FactSet found that incorporating fine-tuned models reduced end-to-end latency by about 60%.

As the system evolved, so did the role of fine-tuning. FactSet accumulated more training data and began updating its models regularly, turning what had been an experimental workflow into a recurring part of developing TTF. Today, the team fine-tunes models roughly every two to three weeks.

Training every few weeks changes the infrastructure requirements. Preparing an environment and configuring GPU compute may be manageable for an occasional experiment. Repeating that work every time new data or a new model is ready to test adds overhead directly to the development cycle.

Model requirements can change from one experiment to the next as well. FactSet has worked with Llama-based models and continues to evaluate newer open models. Different models, prompt lengths, and output characteristics can require different compute configurations, so tying the training environment to a fixed GPU setup would make it harder to adapt as the team experiments.

FactSet uses Databricks AI Runtime to run these fine-tuning workloads on serverless GPU infrastructure. Engineers can choose compute based on the requirements of a particular training run without first provisioning and configuring the underlying GPU environment.

TTF’s training workflow also sits alongside data, experimentation, model management, and governance already running on Databricks. FactSet uses MLflow to track model development and experiments, while its underlying data remains governed within its existing Lakehouse environment.

Running fine-tuning with AI Runtime keeps GPU training inside that workflow. Engineers can work with governed data, train a new model, track the resulting artifacts, and move toward deployment without maintaining a separate GPU stack for fine-tuning. For FactSet, that reduced the time required to set up, train, and deploy a custom TTF model from days to hours.

Databricks' AI Runtime greatly streamlined the process of training a custom Text To Formula (TTF) model. With no infrastructure setup or delays, it was easy to choose the right compute based on prompt size and output token generation. This allowed us to move quickly, maintain our Lakehouse workflows, and deliver a high-quality model with full governance, reducing time to setup, train and deploy our model from days to hours.—Nikhil Sunderraj, Principal Machine Learning Engineer, FactSet Research Systems, Inc.

The ability to change models has been part of TTF’s evolution from the beginning. Advanced RAG, especially reliance solely on externally hosted models, becomes a bottleneck on consistent accuracy and latency as the consumption grows and more complex formulas. RAG worked until the system encountered more complex formulas. Fine-tuned open models gave FactSet another way to improve quality and latency. Now, as newer models become available, the team can evaluate them against the workload rather than treating its current model choice as permanent.

TTF itself is becoming more specialized. As FactSet accumulates more data, the team is exploring additional fine-tuned models for tasks such as query decomposition, component extraction, and library identification. That creates more opportunities to use the model best suited to each part of the workflow, but also makes fast, repeatable training more important.

A model change is much easier to test when it does not require rebuilding the training environment around it. With GPU compute available on demand through AI Runtime, the engineering work shifts toward the questions that actually affect TTF: which model to use, how to train it, and whether the resulting version improves the application.

Additionally, the fine-tuning pipeline was built on Databricks Lakeflow Jobs and Pipelines as a plug-and-play, reusable framework — designed to be easily adopted across different TTF tasks and other teams with minimal setup effort, providing a standardized foundation that reduces onboarding friction and accelerates integration.

Open models are moving quickly. The model that offers the right balance of quality, latency, and cost today may not be the one a team wants six months from now. Preserving model choice therefore requires more than the ability to download a new set of weights. The surrounding training and deployment workflow has to keep up.

FactSet’s experience with TTF shows what that looks like in production. The team can continue testing new open models as its data and application evolve, while AI Runtime provides serverless GPU infrastructure within its existing Databricks workflows. Instead of spending days setting up, training, and deploying each iteration, FactSet can complete that cycle in hours.

For a system that is retrained every few weeks, that difference compounds. New data can move into a new model sooner, and engineers can spend more of each iteration improving TTF rather than preparing the infrastructure required to train it.

entries.title: Power real-time applications and agents with Document Intelligence
entries.summary: At Databricks, our enterprise customers receive millions of documents every single...
entries.content:
Real-time REST APIs for document parsing, extraction, and classification are now Generally Available

by Archika Dogra, Jane Zhang, Zachary Wang and Nihit Desai

  • Document workflows are traditionally built around asynchronous batch pipelines, delaying the operational context needed for immediate downstream decisions in interactive or human-in-the-loop settings.
  • With Document Intelligence real-time REST APIs, your application can read and act on documents as they arrive. Call ai_parse_document, ai_decide, ai_classify, and ai_extract when a file is uploaded, so you can understand what arrived, pull out the information you need, and route it to the right workflow in real-time.
  • Build interactive document workflows with Databricks Apps or custom agents. Embed the REST APIs in applications or agentic workflow automations so documents can turn into business decisions in real-time.

At Databricks, our enterprise customers receive millions of documents every single day. These messy, unstructured documents hold critical context about operations, customers, and finances that power key downstream decisions across the business. Yet when a document arrives, putting that enterprise context to work is surprisingly tedious. For example:

  • A contract lands in an inbox. A legal team member opens it, hunts for the parties, effective date, and renewal terms, then enters them into the system to track the agreement for years.
  • An invoice arrives. An accounts payable specialist finds the vendor, PO number, and total, then enters them into the system so the invoice can go through approval and audit.
  • An insurance claim shows up in a portal with a stack of attachments, and an adjuster reads all of it just to decide where the claim should be routed to.

These are distinct workflows, but they share the same bottleneck: before customers can use the valuable data inside the documents for business analytics or decision-making, someone has to read each document and pull out what matters. That manual step slows everything downstream, and the bottleneck and costs explode as the incoming document volume grows.

Today, the Document Intelligence REST APIs for parsing, classification, and extraction are Generally Available. Our decisions REST API, great for document routing, is launched in beta. Developers can call these APIs from an application or agent when a document arrives, so the workflow can identify what came in, pull out the details it needs, and put them in front of the right person or agent for next steps.

These APIs transform your documents into structured insights in real-time:

  • ai_parse_document reads the file, converts tables and figures into structured text, and calculates citation bounding boxes for downstream processing.
  • ai_decide uses the document’s content to choose what happens next, such as routing the document to a workflow or flagging it for review.
  • ai_extract pulls the fields you specify into a structured result, with optional citations and confidence scores, so humans or agents can check values against the source.
  • ai_classify assigns labels to the document or extracted entities using your business taxonomy with optional rationales and confidence scores.

Example using the ai_extract REST API to extract fields from an invoice:

You can use the REST APIs to bring document understanding into the application where work already happens. For example, with Databricks Apps, you can build a contract intake flow where a lawyer uploads an agreement and opens a review form with the key terms already filled in:

  • Read the contract. 
    ai_parse_document
    turns the file into structured content that the app can save for other uses.
  • Open the right review flow. 
    ai_classify
    identifies whether the agreement is an NDA, MSA, or statement of work, so the app knows which form to show.
  • Prefill the terms. 
    ai_extract
    pulls out the parties, effective date, renewal terms, and notice period. Citations let the lawyer check each value against the source.
  • Move the work forward. The lawyer corrects or approves the fields, and the app writes the reviewed record and source reference to Delta.

Interactive, human-in-the-loop applications are just one way to leverage real-time document processing. You can also call these APIs from a custom agent built on Agent Bricks when it needs to understand or analyze incoming documents before making its next decision.

  • API reference: REST API docs

  • Agent Bricks UI: Try parsing, extraction, and classification interactively from the Agents page in your workspace.

entries.title: Introducing Private Network Gateway
entries.summary: Databricks serverless compute is fully managed, intelligent, and versionless, allowing...
entries.content:
Serverless networking made simple

by Alex Esibov, Manish Bansal, Stanley Wang, Justin Ly and Vijay Raja

  • What is PNG — Private Network Gateway (PNG) is a Databricks-managed gateway that enables easy and secure connectivity from serverless workloads to your private networks and resources at scale.
  • What does it solve — PNG eliminates operational burden by replacing individual connections with one network-level setup — you configure it once, and your existing routes, DNS, and firewall rules decide what's reachable.
  • How can you get started — PNG is now available in Public Preview on Azure and in Private Preview on AWS. Support for Google Cloud is currently in development and coming soon.

Databricks serverless compute is fully managed, intelligent, and versionless, allowing users to focus on solving business problems rather than sizing, tuning, and managing clusters and infrastructure. However, for many teams, the high-friction step that remained was networking: giving serverless compute a private path to databases, applications, and systems inside their own networks. In our customer interviews, more than 75% said their current network configuration and the complexity of dealing with network changes was the main reason specific workloads stayed on classic compute instead of moving to serverless.

Today, we are announcing the public preview of Private Network Gateway (PNG) on Azure, and private preview on AWS. PNG gives your serverless workloads one connection into your network, and from there, you control access to everything your network can already reach.

  • Simplify ingestion across your private databases: use Lakeflow Connect on serverless compute to ingest from supported databases across your VNet/VPC and connected on-premises environments
  • Connect AI agents to private services: An agent you build on Databricks can call a private MCP server you host
  • Use your own package repositories: Serverless can install Python libraries from a private PyPI, Artifactory, or Nexus repository inside your network
  • Route egress through your own firewall: Send traffic through your existing firewall or content inspection service, so egress is filtered and logged natively with your own tools
  • Keep a consistent, customer-owned source IP: Your SaaS apps like Salesforce, can see a source IP that belongs to you

Each of these used to require coordinated deployment between networking, security, and admin teams, and multiple new deployments like load balancers and proxy VMs. With PNG, you configure one connection, and the resources your network can reach become reachable from serverless. PNG scales by network, not by endpoint.

Private Network Gateway has significantly simplified how we connect serverless compute to data sources on Azure and on-premises — no more standing up a private link service and load balancer for every connection. It also brings real flexibility to our serverless operations: we can reuse an existing workspace subnet, which makes firewall approvals easier, while still controlling exactly which destinations are reachable.—Fabiano Seki, Tech Lead, Data Engineering, Banco Bradesco

Classic compute runs inside your own virtual network, so reaching your data is straightforward: you peer the networks using standard cloud primitives. In contrast, serverless runs in a Databricks-managed network, which, on one hand removes the operational overhead, but it also means your private resources need an explicit path.

Serverless Private Link provides that path, and it remains the right tool for cloud-managed services like AWS S3, or Azure Data Lake Storage. But for resources you host and manage, like databases, Kafka clusters, or internal APIs, connecting often meant a separate private endpoint, load balancer, and proxy VM for each resource — plus back-and-forth coordination between your Databricks admin, cloud admin, and network security team. For a handful of resources, this may be manageable. But when a team needs serverless to access dozens of databases, APIs, and internal services; across VNets, peered networks, and on-premises environments, the per-resource approach quickly becomes a bottleneck, making it painful, slow, and manually intensive.

The setup is easy and straightforward: You delegate one subnet in your virtual network to Databricks and PNG establishes a managed, encrypted gateway from serverless compute into that subnet. You configure the gateway inside a Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC), the same account-level object you already use for serverless networking. You can then attach the NCC to your workspaces, and supported serverless workloads can reach the private destinations you allow.

There are no gateway VMs for you to deploy, patch, or scale in your network. Databricks creates and runs the gateway for you. You keep control of your network.

Before PNG, enabling private connectivity for Databricks Serverless required significant network setup and coordination. PNG simplified the whole process, reduced operational overhead, and helped us run jobs faster—making serverless much easier to integrate into our existing environment.—Primož Gale, Lead Technical Architect, NLB

PNG keeps the network boundary with you:

  • Your gateway is yours: it provides a dedicated path into your network, not a shared appliance carrying other customers' traffic. Isolation is enforced via encapsulation and network security rules.
  • The gateway enforces workspace-level access controls before any traffic leaves.
  • Beyond the subnet, your route tables, network security groups, DNS resolvers, and security appliances decide what serverless can reach, the same way they do for the rest of your network.

You choose how much traffic PNG carries, through two modes:

  • specific_destinations
    sends only the fully qualified domain names you list through PNG. All other traffic keeps its normal path. Use this when you want precise control over which resources serverless can reach.
  • all_traffic
    routes outbound traffic through your network, except anything matching a more-specific Private Link or service-endpoint path, which keeps its native route. Use this mode to inspect broad egress through your own firewall, or to send it out through your own IP addresses.

PNG is additive. It sits alongside the private connectivity and egress controls you already use for Databricks and does not change them, so you can enable or remove it without affecting your existing setup.

Before Private Network Gateway, managing secrets and network connectivity for serverless workloads required multiple integrations and ongoing coordination. Today, with PNG, we can securely access internal services directly and centrally manage outbound traffic through our existing controls, making operations simpler, faster, and easier to govern.—Michel Schwandner, Platform Engineer, Julius Blum GmbH

Private Network Gateway is now available in Public Preview on Azure, and in Private Preview on AWS. Support for Google Cloud is in development.
